title: Une couronne pour Samuel  (A Wreath for Samuel)

segments.t: We begin at a florist's. Andréa, the toughest agent at ASK, is ordering a funeral wreath for Samuel, with Françoise Fabian beside her. Françoise was Samuel's client, and she is supposed to start a film by the director Gabor Rajevski in three weeks. You'll hear the story in French first; there's no need to catch every word.
Et la cause du décès?
Il a avalé une guêpe.
Andréa, Samuel est mort. J'ai perdu un ami très cher.
Je sais, Françoise. Moi aussi.
Mais j'ai aussi perdu mon agent.
Je comprends. Je suis prête à prendre la relève.
Ce film... Je ne crois pas que je vais le faire.
Le tournage commence dans trois semaines.
C'est un film très sombre. J'ai besoin d'optimisme.
Pensez à Samuel.
Je veux voir ma fille, voyager.
Soyons professionnels.
Vous n'avez pas de famille. J'ai une vie.
Mais des gens comptent sur ce film!
À quel âge ces caprices s'arrêtent-ils?
Désolée.
Pourquoi je reste dans cette agence?
Oui, c'est parfait.
Let's go back through it slowly. The wreath is nearly ready, the florist asks for the name for the ribbon, and then Françoise asks the question everyone in Paris is asking.
Et la cause du décès?
'And the cause of death?' A rather formal word for death, the kind you see on official papers. Françoise has heard some wild rumours from Rio, and Andréa sets her straight.
Il a avalé une guêpe.
'He swallowed a wasp.' This is the everyday past tense: the helper verb 'to have' plus the past form of the verb. Françoise remarks that you can live an exciting life and still die in a silly way.
Andréa, Samuel est mort.
'Andréa, Samuel is dead.' Said simply, between two people who both loved him.
J'ai perdu un ami très cher.
'I've lost a very dear friend.' The same past tense again: 'I have lost'.
Je sais, Françoise. Moi aussi.
'I know, Françoise. So have I.' Literally 'me too'. Andréa and Françoise use the polite 'you' with each other all through the scene.
Mais j'ai aussi perdu mon agent.
'But I've also lost my agent.' And now we see where this is going: business.
Je suis prête à prendre la relève.
'I'm ready to take over.' The word for 'ready' has a feminine ending because Andréa is a woman. Taking over means taking over as her agent.
Je ne crois pas que je vais le faire.
'I don't think I'm going to do it.' Françoise means the film by Gabor Rajevski. Notice the near future again: 'to go' plus a plain verb. That's the bombshell.
Le tournage commence dans trois semaines.
'The shoot starts in three weeks.' The whole film depends on her.
J'ai besoin d'optimisme.
'I need optimism.' Literally 'I have need of optimism'. That's a very useful pattern: 'to have need of' followed by what you need.
Pensez à Samuel.
'Think of Samuel.' A polite command, ending in the formal 'you' form. Andréa tries an emotional argument.
Je veux voir ma fille, voyager.
'I want to see my daughter, to travel.' Françoise has other plans for her life.
Soyons professionnels.
'Let's be professional.' This is a 'let's' command, made from the 'we' form of the verb 'to be'. Andréa switches to business.
Vous n'avez pas de famille. J'ai une vie.

'You have no family. I have a life.' Françoise turns it round on Andréa: you only have your job. Notice 'no family': after a negative, French replaces 'a' or 'some' with the short word that normally means 'of'.
Mais des gens comptent sur ce film!
'But people are counting on this film!' Andréa is losing patience, and then she goes much too far.
À quel âge ces caprices s'arrêtent-ils?

'At what age do these whims stop?' A whim is a sudden fancy. Here the verb and the little word for 'they' swap places, which is the formal, written way to ask a question. Saying this to a great actress of about eighty is a disaster.
Désolée.
'Sorry.' Andréa realises it immediately. She is a woman, so on paper the word gets an extra e.
Pourquoi je reste dans cette agence?
'Why do I stay with this agency?' A question with no change of word order at all: in speech, just raise your voice at the end.
Oui, c'est parfait.
'Yes, it's perfect.' The florist shows them the finished wreath, and after that conversation, nothing is really perfect. Now listen to the whole scene again, from the cause of death to the wreath.
Et la cause du décès?
Il a avalé une guêpe.
Andréa, Samuel est mort. J'ai perdu un ami très cher.
Je sais, Françoise. Moi aussi.
Mais j'ai aussi perdu mon agent.
Je comprends. Je suis prête à prendre la relève.
Ce film... Je ne crois pas que je vais le faire.
Le tournage commence dans trois semaines.
C'est un film très sombre. J'ai besoin d'optimisme.
Pensez à Samuel.
Je veux voir ma fille, voyager.
Soyons professionnels.
Vous n'avez pas de famille. J'ai une vie.
Mais des gens comptent sur ce film!
À quel âge ces caprices s'arrêtent-ils?
Désolée.
Pourquoi je reste dans cette agence?
Oui, c'est parfait.
That's the start of the episode: a funeral to plan and a star who wants to walk away. If some lines went by fast, that's normal; you'll recognise them when you watch. Until next time.
Bonne journée!
